newsitem.title: USA: Thousands flee California towns as levee breaks.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flee California towns as levee breaks.

text.p: Thousands of people were ordered to evacuate their homes in four northern California towns late on Thursday in an area where a levee on the rain-swollen Feather River broke, officials said.
The large-scale evacuation was the latest crisis caused by a week of torrential storms that have caused floods, mudslides and power outages in California, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon and Washington state.

The mandatory evacuation orders affected the towns of Marysville, Yuba City, Linda and Olivehurst, clustered close to the Feather River about 50 miles (80 kms) northeast of Sacramento, officials said. Eighteen evacuation shelters were opened for the evacuees.
"We're doing all we can to cope with a real difficult situation," Bill Harris, a spokesman for the Yuba County Office of Emergency Services, said.

Together, the towns have a population of around 65,000 people, but an unknown number had already left in the last two days when residents were being advised to leave but the order was not mandatory, officials said. It was not known how many left on Thursday night but officials said they could number in the thousands or tens of thousands.

Authorities ordered the evacuation of Marysville and Yuba City on Thursday evening because they were concerned whether levees would hold. Two hours later, a levee along the Feather River broke near Olivehurst and mandatory evacuations were ordered in Linda and Olivehurst, Harris said.
He said the levee broke in a rural area, spilling water into fields, and no immediate flooding was reported in the towns.

Sheriff's deputies went through the towns ordering people through loudspeakers to leave, Harris said. Townspeople grabbed what they could and left in a stream of vehicles. There were no reports of deaths or injuries.
Earlier on Thursday, California Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency in 25 northern California counties hit by the storms, making them eligible for state aid.

In Nevada, the normally placid Truckee river overflowed, causing the worst flooding in downtown Reno in more than 40 years. A fast-moving torrent of murky brown water swept through homes and businesses, leaving a basketball net and street signs just poking out above the flood.

Several Reno hotel-casinos were forced to close and evacuate guests, but in others, the gambling went on in sandbagged casinos. Runways at the Reno-Tahoe airport were submerged and several airliners stood in water.
After touring the area by helicopter, Nevada Gov. Bob Miller, who declared a state of emergency in four counties, said damage could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

"It's clear to say this is the most significant flood damage in the history of Nevada in terms of financial cost," he said. Miller said he had contacted the Federal Emergency Management Agency in hopes of getting speedy approval for federal aid for flood victims.
In northern California's wine country, the Russian and Napa rivers broke their banks in places, flooding the town of Guerneville and inundating vineyards.
Emergency officials advised the 4,000 residents of the Pajaro area in central California to evacuate as soon as possible because the Pajaro River was nearing flood stage.

Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber declared emergencies in five storm-hit counties and Gov. Mike Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 19 Washington counties. At least 14 deaths are blamed on the storms, estimated to have caused up to $250 million in property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California alone.

About 2,300 tourists, park workers and their families were stranded in California's scenic Yosemite National Park, 150 miles (240 km) southeast of San Francisco, when the Merced River flooded, closing all highways into Yosemite Valley, where the park headquarters and accommodations are located, officials said.
